---
title: "Sound 11: Reverb"
toc: true
toc-depth: 2
---

Clap in a cathedral and the sound goes on for seconds after your hands stop. It bounces off the walls,
the floor and the ceiling, thousands of times, each echo a little quieter and a little duller, until
they blur into a smooth wash. That wash is **reverberation**, and every room has its own. A **reverb**
effect puts a dry recording into a room that isn't there.

**How to use the page.** The source starts as **single hits**, so you can hear each hit's tail die
away. The strip under the controls is the room's **impulse response**: what one instant click would
sound like in this room.

## The room

<div class="sk" data-w="reverb" data-source="hits"></div>

- **Decay time (RT60)**: how long the tail takes to fall by 60 dB, which is about until you can't hear
  it. A living room is about 0.5 s, a concert hall about 2 s, a cathedral 5 s or more.
- **Pre-delay**: the gap before the reverb starts. In a big room the first reflection takes a while
  to come back. A little pre-delay keeps a voice clear in front of its reverb.
- **Damping**: in real rooms the high frequencies die first, absorbed by air, carpet and people. Lower
  damping makes a darker, warmer tail.
- **Early reflections**: the first few distinct echoes from the nearest walls. They tell your ear how
  big the room is before the tail arrives.
- **Mix**: how far away the sound seems. More wet signal pushes it to the back of the room.

Try the presets: a small room, a hall, a cathedral, a **plate** (a big steel sheet with a pickup, used
in studios since the 1950s: bright and dense, no early reflections) and **reverse**, the impulse response
played backwards so each sound swells *into* itself.

## How it is made: convolution

This reverb is a **convolution reverb**. It needs one thing: the impulse response of the room. To
capture a real room, engineers play a click (or a sweep) in it and record what comes back. The
computer then replays that recording once for every sample of the input, scaled by that sample's
level, and adds them all up. That's a lot of arithmetic, which the browser does for us.

The impulse responses here aren't recordings. They are made from decaying [noise](sound-noise.qmd)
that gets duller as it fades, plus a few early reflections. That's close to what a real room does, and
it means every control can change the room instantly.

## On music

Switch the source to the **chords**, the **drum loop** or your **microphone** (headphones on). Long
reverb makes chords smooth and huge but turns drums to mush; fast music wants short reverb or a lot of
pre-delay. Singing into the cathedral preset and listening to your own voice come back is the best way
to learn what reverb does.
